passages.title: All creation glorifies the sovereign Lord
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat are the opening of Sūrah al-Ḥadīd, and they are one sustained portrait of Allah: the universe is already declaring His purity, and the passage then unfolds *why* — because the kingdom is His, because He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden, because He created the heavens and the earth and rose over the Throne, because nothing enters the earth or leaves it, descends or ascends, without His knowledge, and because He is with you wherever you are. What holds the six ayat together is a single movement: from creation's worship (ayah 1) to the Owner's absolute power (ayah 2), to His very Being (ayah 3), to His all-encompassing knowledge and presence (ayat 4–6). By the end, the reader has been walked from the outermost edge of the heavens to the secrets inside his own chest.

## "Glorification has been declared" — the word the sūrah opens with

Ayah 1 opens with *sabbaḥa* — a past-tense verb: glorification *has been* proclaimed to Allah by whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes something easy to miss. This sūrah belongs to a group of five that the scholars call **al-Musabbiḥāt** — sūrahs that begin with the glorification of Allah: al-Ḥadīd, al-Ḥashr, aṣ-Ṣaff, al-Jumuʿah and at-Taghābun. The first three open in the past perfect tense, *sabbaḥa* ("purity has been proclaimed"), while the last two open in the imperfect tense, *yusabbiḥu* ("purity is proclaimed"). Citing Mazharī, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the point out: taken together, the two tenses imply that Allah's purity is to be declared **at all times — the past, the present and the future**.

*Tasbīḥ* is the declaring of Allah's purity — which is why Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders *sabbaḥa* as "purity has been proclaimed." So the sūrah does not begin by telling you to do it. It begins by informing you that it is already being done — and by everything.

**Ibn Kathīr on the sweep of ayah 1:** everything that exists in the heavens and earth praises and glorifies Him, *including creatures and plants*. He brings the parallel from Sūrat al-Isrāʼ: "The seven heavens and the earth and all that is therein, glorify Him and there is not a thing but glorifies His praise. But you understand not their glorification" (17:44). That last clause is the humbling part. The praise is real; our perception of it is the thing that falls short.

**Two names close the ayah.** Ibn Kathīr explains *al-ʿAzīz* (the Almighty) as the One to Whom all things submit in humility, and *al-Ḥakīm* (the All-Wise) as wise **in His creating, His commanding, and His legislating**. Notice how that pairing works: might without wisdom would be raw force; wisdom without might would be good intention with no power to enact it. In Him, both are perfect, and the wisdom runs through all three domains — the world He made, the orders He issues, and the law He gives.

## Ayah 2: ownership that is total

"His is the kingdom of the heavens and the earth. It is He Who gives life and causes death; and He is Able to do all things."

Ibn Kathīr: He is **the absolute Owner of His creation**, bringing life and death, and granting what He wills to whom He wills. And *He is Able to do all things* means, in his words: whatever He wills, is; and whatever He does not will, will never be.

Sit with that second half. It is a complete theory of what happens in the world, in eleven words. Nothing that occurred needed His permission twice, and nothing that failed to occur was ever going to.

## Ayah 3: the ayah better than a thousand

**A hadith frames this whole passage.** Imam Ahmad recorded that ʿIrbāḍ bin Sāriyah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to recite al-Musabbiḥāt before he went to sleep, saying: *"In them there is an ayah that is better than a thousand ayat."* Abū Dāwūd, at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʼī collected this hadith; at-Tirmidhī said, *"Ḥasan Gharīb."* Ibn Kathīr identifies the ayah referred to — and Allah knows best — as ayah 3 of this sūrah, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same identification from him:

> "He is al-Awwal and al-Ākhir, aẓ-Ẓāhir and al-Bāṭin. And He is the All-Knower of everything."

Four names, in two opposed pairs. Ibn Kathīr reports that there are **about ten and some odd number of different sayings** collected from the scholars of tafsīr explaining this ayah; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that these interpretations are **not contradictory** — the scope is wide enough to accommodate them all. That is itself a lesson in how to read a verse about Allah's Being: not by narrowing it, but by letting it be as wide as it is.

**Al-Awwal, the First.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: the meaning of this attribute is more or less fixed — that ontologically there was nothing before Allah; He created everything and He is the First Cause of all existent things.

**Al-Ākhir, the Last.** He will exist even after everything else has perished, as the ayah testifies: "Everything has to perish except His Countenance" (28:88). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān handles a fair objection here: Paradise, Hell, and those who enter them are not going to be annihilated — so how is everything described as perishing? The answer is that perishing covers two possibilities, *actual* and *potential*. Some creatures will actually perish on the Day of Judgment; others will not actually perish but retain the **inherent capacity for death and destruction**. So despite being existent they may still be described as *hālik* or *fānī* — perishing. Only the Supreme Being of Allah is such that non-existence has never occurred to Him, nor can death overtake Him. That is the force of *al-Ākhir*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also records a second, different explanation from **Imām al-Ghazālī** (transmitted via *Rūḥ ul Maʿānī*), which approaches *al-Ākhir* from the angle of *maʿrifah* (knowledge of Allah): knowing Allah is the ultimate goal a person hopes to achieve, and he moves toward it, passing through all the different stages and stations, until he attains that Divine Knowledge. Allah is *the Last* in the sense of being the final destination of the seeker's journey.

**Aẓ-Ẓāhir, the Manifest.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: a Being whose manifestation is superior to everything. Since manifestation is an offshoot of existence, and the Existence of Allah is First and superior to all existent entities, the Divine Manifestation surpasses the manifestation of all other beings. Nothing in this universe is more manifest than Him — the manifestation of His wisdom and His power is visible in every particle of this world.

**Al-Bāṭin, the Hidden.** The accurate nature and essence of Allah's Being is hidden, in the sense that the Divine Essence (*dhāt*) is beyond human perception. No intellect and no thought can ever reach the accurate and intrinsic Essence of Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lets Persian poetry carry what prose cannot: that He is far beyond any hypothesis, any guess, any assumption, any imagination, and far beyond whatever we have ever seen, heard or read about — and that whatever example we cite to explain Him is no more than a sheer failure.

That is the boundary Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws and does not cross. The two names, held together, mark out both sides of it: His manifestation surpasses everything manifest, and His Essence lies beyond the reach of any intellect.

**Ibn Kathīr adds a narrower reading.** He quotes al-Bukhārī, who said: "Yaḥyā said, '*Aẓ-Ẓāhir*: knowing all things; *al-Bāṭin*: knowing all things.'" Ibn Kathīr's shaykh, al-Ḥāfiẓ al-Mizzī, identified this Yaḥyā as Ibn Ziyād al-Farrāʼ, who authored a book entitled *Maʿānī al-Qurʼān*. Reported as one saying among the ten-odd — a good example of how the classical scholars preserved differing views rather than flattening them.

### The ayah as medicine for doubt

Abū Dāwūd recorded that Abū Zamīl said: *"I mentioned to Ibn ʿAbbās that I felt something in my heart. He said, 'Doubts?' and then laughed."* Then Ibn ʿAbbās said, "No one can escape this," and recited Allah's words, "So if you are in doubt concerning that which We have revealed to you, then ask those who are reading the Book before you. Verily, the truth has come to you from your Lord" (10:94). And he said to him: **"When you feel any of this in your heart, recite** 'He is al-Awwal and al-Ākhir, aẓ-Ẓāhir and al-Bāṭin. And He is the All-Knower of everything.'"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits the same prescription from Ibn ʿAbbās: if Shayṭān casts an evil scruple into anyone's heart and thus causes skepticism about Allah and the religion of truth, he should **softly recite this ayah**.

Two things are worth noticing. First, Ibn ʿAbbās *laughed* — the intrusive thought was not treated as catastrophe or as proof of hypocrisy; as he said, no one escapes it. Second, the remedy prescribed is not argument but recitation: intrusive doubt is answered by turning the heart back to the greatness of the One being doubted.

### How the Prophet ﷺ prayed with these names at night

Ibn Kathīr notes that there are hadiths mentioned about this. Among them, Imam Ahmad recorded that Abū Hurayrah said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would recite this supplication while going to bed:

> "O Allah, Lord of the seven heavens and Lord of the Magnificent Throne! Our Lord, and the Lord of everything, Revealer of the Tawrāh, the Injīl and the Furqān, the Splitter of the grain of corn and the date stone! I seek refuge with You from the evil of everything whose forehead You have control over. O Allah! **You are al-Awwal, nothing is before You; al-Ākhir, nothing is after You; aẓ-Ẓāhir, nothing is above You; and al-Bāṭin, nothing is below You.** Remove the burden of debt from us and free us from poverty."

Ibn Kathīr adds that Muslim recorded this hadith via Sahl, who said that Abū Ṣāliḥ used to order them to lie on their right side when about to sleep and then say it — and he used to narrate that from Abū Hurayrah from the Prophet ﷺ.

Look at what the supplication does with the four names of ayah 3: it glosses each in a single short clause, denying that anything could stand before, after, above or below Allah. And then — strikingly — the prayer descends from the Throne to a household worry: *remove our debt, free us from poverty*. The One who has no before and no after is the same One you ask about the bills.

## Ayah 4: creation, the Throne, and knowledge that misses nothing

"He it is Who created the heavens and the earth in six Days and then rose (*istawā*) over the Throne."

Ibn Kathīr states that Allah created the heavens and earth, and all that is between them, in six Days and then rose over the Throne after He created them. He does not expand on the meaning here — he says he discussed it before in the explanation of Sūrat al-Aʿrāf, so it is not necessary to repeat it. We will follow him in that restraint and say no more about it here than he did.

Then the ayah turns to knowledge, in four directions — down, up, in, out:

- **What goes into the earth** — Ibn Kathīr: His knowledge of the amount of seeds and drops of water that enter inside the earth's surface.
- **What comes forth from it** — plants, vegetation and fruits.
- **What descends from the heaven** — rain, snow, hail, and whatever Allah decides descends from heaven of decisions and commandments brought down by the honourable angels.
- **What ascends thereto** — angels and deeds. Ibn Kathīr cites a hadith found in the Ṣaḥīḥ in which the Prophet ﷺ said: *"To Him ascend the deeds of the night before the day falls and the deeds of the day before the night falls."*

He brings the great parallel from al-Anʿām: "And with Him are the keys of all that is hidden, none knows them but He. And He knows whatever there is in the land and in the sea; not a leaf falls, but He knows it. There is not a grain in the darkness of the earth nor anything fresh or dry, but is written in a Clear Record" (6:59).

### "And He is with you wheresoever you may be"

Ibn Kathīr explains this as: He is watching over you and witnessing your deeds wherever you may be — **on land or at sea, during the night or the day, at home or in open areas or deserts**. All of that is the same before His knowledge, and all of it is under His sight and hearing. He hears your speech and sees where you are; He knows your secrets and your public statements. He supports this with "even when they cover themselves with their garments, He knows what they conceal and what they reveal" (11:5), and "It is the same whether any of you conceals his speech or declares it openly, whether he be hid by night or goes forth freely by day" (13:10).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān guards this carefully: **no man is able to comprehend the essential nature of Allah's company or His being with us**, though it is absolutely true that He is with us — because no man can exist or do any work without it, since the Divine Will (*mashiyyah*) and power are necessary for everything. Therefore Allah is with every human being, in every situation, at every place. And it closes the point the way the scholars close such points: *Allah knows best.*

Ibn Kathīr draws the practical conclusion by citing the hadith found in the Ṣaḥīḥ in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ answered Jibrīl when he asked him about *iḥsān* (excellence in worship): **"To worship Allah as if you see Him, and even though you cannot see Him, He surely sees you."** That is what ayah 4 asks of you. Not a doctrine about divine surveillance — a way of standing, sitting, working and speaking.

## Ayah 5: everything comes back

"His is the kingdom of the heavens and the earth. And to Allah return all the matters."

The ownership statement of ayah 2 returns, and Ibn Kathīr reads this as asserting that Allah is **the King and Owner of this life and the Hereafter**, citing "And truly, unto Us belong the last and the first" (92:13), and the praise-verses 28:70 and 34:1. Everyone in the heavens and the earth is a servant before Him and humble: "There is none in the heavens and the earth but comes unto the Most Gracious as a servant... And every one of them will come to Him alone on the Day of Resurrection" (19:93–95).

So *"to Allah return all the matters"* means all matters will be referred to Him on the Day of Resurrection, and He will judge His creation as He wills. Ibn Kathīr then makes the point that turns this from a warning into a comfort: **indeed, He is the Most Just, Who never falls into injustice, not even the weight of a speck of dust**; if one performs even one good deed, Allah will multiply it up to ten times, and "gives from Him a great reward" (4:40); and "We shall set up Balances of justice on the Day of Resurrection, then none will be dealt with unjustly in anything. And if there be the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it" (21:47).

The knowledge described in ayah 4 and the judgment described in ayah 5 are the same fact seen twice: nothing is missed, so nothing is lost — neither the wrong done to you nor the good you did that no one noticed.

## Ayah 6: the turning of night and day, and the secret in the chest

"He merges night into day, and merges day into night, and He has full knowledge of whatsoever is in the breasts."

Ibn Kathīr: this means He does what He wills with His creatures. He alternates the night and day and measures them by His wisdom, as He wills — sometimes the night is longer than the day, sometimes the opposite, sometimes their length is equal; and sometimes He makes the season winter, then changes it to spring, then summer, then autumn. All this He does by His wisdom and His due measure of everything in His creation.

And then the sūrah's opening closes where you least expect: *"and He has full knowledge of whatsoever is in the breasts"* — He knows the secrets, Ibn Kathīr says, no matter how concealed they are. The passage began with the heavens and the earth and ends inside your ribcage. The same wisdom that lengthens a night by a minute knows the thought you have not admitted to yourself.

## Living it

- **Join the tasbīḥ that is already happening.** Ayah 1 says creation is doing this; the tenses of the Musabbiḥāt say Allah's purity is to be declared at all times. Your *subḥān Allah* is not adding something new to the universe — it is you catching up with it.
- **Use ayah 3 the way Ibn ʿAbbās prescribed.** When doubt whispers, do not debate it in your head — recite "He is al-Awwal and al-Ākhir, aẓ-Ẓāhir and al-Bāṭin, and He is the All-Knower of everything," softly, and let the greatness of the One being doubted answer the whisper.
- **Take the Prophet's ﷺ bedtime supplication as it is.** Say the four clauses as he ﷺ said them, and bring your debt and your poverty into the same breath as the Throne.
- **Live ayah 4 as iḥsān.** He is with you on land or at sea, at home or in the open desert — so worship Him as if you see Him, knowing that even though you cannot see Him, He surely sees you.
- **Rest on ayah 5.** Every matter is referred back to the One who never falls into injustice by a speck's weight, and who multiplies a single good deed up to ten times.

passages.title: Believe and spend from what He entrusted
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat take two things — believing and giving — and refuse to let them come apart. Allah commands faith and spending together in ayah 7, then asks twice, almost incredulously, *why not?* — why do you not believe (ayah 8), why do you not spend (ayah 10) — before offering, in ayah 11, an astonishing invitation: that the Owner of everything will accept a loan from you.

Underneath runs a single idea: **nothing in your hand is finally yours.** The wealth was entrusted, the heavens and the earth revert to Allah, and the only portion of your property you actually keep is the portion you sent ahead.

## "Spend of that whereof He has made you trustees" (ayah 7)

The command in ayah 7 is *āminū* — believe — and *anfiqū* — spend. Ibn Kathir reads it as an order to have **perfect faith in Allah and in His Messenger, and that one should persist on this path, adhering firmly to it**: not a one-off assent but a standing posture. And the spending is not out of "your" wealth. The Arabic says *mimmā jaʿalakum mustakhlafīna fīhi* — "of that whereof He has made you *mustakhlafīn*."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the word has two meanings:

- **Deputies.** The interpretation of the majority of commentators: the wealth held by human beings originally belongs to Allah, but He has made them His deputies to use it according to His directions — allowed to use it for their own benefit, but always subject to the rules He prescribed in the Sharīʿah. Mufti Muhammad Taqi Usmani draws the conclusion: once it is believed that one is not the absolute owner of this wealth, it should not be difficult to spend according to the command of its absolute Owner.
- **Successors.** Some other exegetes take *mustakhlafīn* in the sense of "successors": whatever wealth we hold today reached us from other people who owned it before us, and ultimately it will pass on to others through inheritance or some other mode of transfer. All kinds of wealth are in transit — so one should not hesitate to spend it in Allah's way, since it has to pass on in any case.

Ibn Kathir's own comments sound both notes. Allah, he says, encourages spending from what He has made mankind trustees of — **the wealth that He has lent you**, which was in the hands of those before you and was later transferred to you. Spend from it as Allah commanded; otherwise He will hold you accountable for ignoring what He ordained on you in this regard. And the phrase itself indicates that **you will surrender this wealth to someone else**. Those who inherit from you might obey Allah with it, and so acquire more happiness than you; or they might disobey Allah with it, in which case **you will have helped them commit evil and transgression**.

**From the Sunnah.** Imam Ahmad recorded that ʿAbdullāh bin Ash-Shikhkhīr said: "I came to Allah's Messenger ﷺ as he was reciting and saying, *alhākum at-takāthur* — (abundance diverts you) (102:1) —

*(The Son of ʿAdam claims, "My wealth, my wealth." But is there anything belonging to you, except that which you consumed, which you used, or which you wore and then it became worn or you gave as charity and sent it forward?)*

Muslim also collected it, with the addition: *(Other than that, you will go away from it and leave it behind for other people.)*

Hence the closing promise of ayah 7 — *"And such of you as believe and spend, theirs will be a great reward"* — which Ibn Kathir says encourages having faith and spending in acts of obedience.

## "What is the matter with you that you believe not?" (ayah 8)

Ayah 8 turns from command to remonstration: *"And what is the matter with you that you believe not in Allah! While the Messenger invites you to believe in your Lord; and He has indeed taken your covenant, if you are real believers."* Ibn Kathir gives its force: **"what prevents you from believing, while the Messenger is among you calling you to faith and bringing forward clear proofs and evidences that affirm the truth of what he brought you?"**

Ibn Kathir then mentions a hadith he had reported at the beginning of his explanation on the chapter on Faith in Sahih Al-Bukhari. One day the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to his Companions:

*(Who do you consider among the believers as having the most amazing faith?)*

They said, "The angels." He said: *(And what prevents them from believing when they are with their Lord?)*

They said, "Then the Prophets." He said: *(What prevents them from believing when the revelation comes down to them?)*

They said, "Then us." He said: *(What prevents you from believing, when I am amongst you? Actually, the believers who have the most amazing faith, are some people who will come after you; they will find pages that they will believe in.)*

The most amazing faith belongs to people who come afterwards and believe from the written page. That is us.

**The covenant.** *"And He has indeed taken your covenant" (mīthāq).* The sources give three explanations:

- Ibn Kathir says this is similar to another statement of Allah: *"And remember Allah's favor to you and His covenant with which He bound you when you said: 'We hear and we obey.'"* (5:7) — which refers to giving the pledge of allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ.
- **Ibn Jarir** said the covenant mentioned here is that taken from mankind when they were still in Adam's loin; this is also the opinion of **Mujāhid** — and, Ibn Kathir adds, *Allah knows best*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies this as the covenant of *alast*, described in 7:172–174: Allah gathered all the souls even before they took the form of their existence and asked them, *"Am I not your Lord?"* They replied: *"Of course You are, we affirm."*
- Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a further possibility: the pledge taken from the previous prophets and their followers to believe in the final Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and support him — the covenant of 3:81: *"…then comes to you a messenger verifying what is with you; you shall have to believe in him and you shall have to support him. He said: 'Do you affirm and accept my covenant in this respect?' They said: 'We affirm.'"*

**"If you are real believers."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the difficulty: the earlier part of the ayah reprimands people for *not* believing, so how is it appropriate to end by addressing them as believers? The answer: the unbelievers did not deny the existence of the Creator. They claimed to believe in Him — hence their own words, *"We only worship them [the idols] that they may bring us nearer to Allah in position"* (39:3). So the closing phrase implies: **if your claim to believe is true, then go the perfect and right way in believing** — which is not only to believe in Allah but also to believe in His Messenger ﷺ.

## "He sends down manifest Ayat" (ayah 9)

Ayah 9 removes every excuse. *"It is He Who sends down manifest Ayat to His servant"* — **clear proofs, unequivocal evidences and plain attestations**, as Ibn Kathir glosses them — *"that He may bring you out from darkness into light"*: **from the darkness of ignorance, disbelief and contradictory statements to the light of guidance, certainty and faith.**

Then: *"And verily, Allah is to you full of kindness (Raʾūf), Most Merciful (Raḥīm)."* Ibn Kathir locates that mercy concretely — **by revealing the Divine Books and sending the Messengers to guide mankind, eradicating doubts and removing confusion.** Guidance itself is the tenderness.

## "What is the matter with you that you spend not?" (ayah 10)

*"And what is the matter with you that you spend not in the cause of Allah? And to Allah belongs the heritage of the heavens and the earth."*

Ibn Kathir's reading is direct: it means **spend, and do not fear poverty or scarcity.** Surely, He in whose cause you spent is the King and Owner of the heavens and earth and has perfect control over their every affair, including their treasuries. He is the Owner of the Throne, and He is the One who said *"And whatsoever you spend of anything, He will replace it. And He is the best of providers"* (34:39), and *"whatever is with you, will be exhausted, and whatever is with Allah will remain"* (16:96). Therefore, Ibn Kathir concludes, **those who trust in and depend on Allah will spend, and they will not fear poverty or destitution coming to them from the Owner of the Throne. They know that Allah will surely compensate them for whatever they spend.**

**Why "inheritance"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on the word *mīrāth*. Inheritance transfers automatically by virtue of the law of the Sharīʿah, and the deceased has no choice in the matter. Allah describes His ownership of the heavens and the earth with this word presumably because all those assets deemed to be owned by men will ultimately return to Allah, **no matter whether men like it or not**. He transferred part-ownership of things to man by His grace; but on the Day of Judgement even this outward and partial ownership will no longer remain in anyone's hands. The conclusion: since those who are apparently owners today will be compensated in the Hereafter for what they spend in Allah's way, anything spent in His way **becomes the eternal property of the spender**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites, from Mazharī, a report recorded in Tirmidhī on the authority of Sayyidah ʿĀʼishah. One day a goat was slaughtered and most of it was distributed among other people, except for a foreleg. The Prophet ﷺ wanted to know from her whether any part of it was spared from distribution. She said, "Yes, a foreleg." The Prophet ﷺ said: **"The entire goat is spared, except this foreleg."**

## The Conquest as the dividing line (ayah 10)

The second half of ayah 10 ranks the givers: *"Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquering. Such are higher in degree than those who spent and fought afterwards. But to all Allah has promised the best."*

**Which conquest?** The majority considers it the conquest of Makkah. **Ash-Shaʿbī** and several others said the ayah refers to the treaty at Al-Hudaybiyyah. Ibn Kathir notes proof for this second opinion in a hadith from Anas collected by Imam Ahmad. Anas said: "Khalid bin Al-Walid and ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin ʿAwf had a dispute. Khalid said to ʿAbdur-Raḥmān, 'You boast about days (battles) that you participated in before us.' When the news of this statement reached the Prophet ﷺ he said:

*(Do not bother my Companions, for by He in Whose Hand is my soul! If you spend an amount of gold equal to (Mount) Uhud, (or equal to the mountains), you will not reach the level of their actions.)*"

Ibn Kathir then states the historical fact that carries the argument: **it is a known fact that Khalid bin Al-Walid, whom the Prophet addressed this statement to, embraced Islam during the period between the treaty of Al-Hudaybiyyah and the conquering of Makkah.**

**Why the early ones rank higher.** Ibn Kathir puts it plainly: before Makkah was conquered, things were difficult for Muslims and only the righteous ones embraced Islam; after Makkah was conquered, Islam spread tremendously and people embraced the religion of Allah en masse. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān expands this into a study of human nature: wise men of the world will not join a movement where there is a fear of defeat or annihilation — they wait for results and join when the movement shows signs of success. Those who embraced Islam **before** the conquest did so while the Muslims were very small in number and weak and persecuted, when disclosing one's faith could amount to losing one's life, hearth and home. Those who came later are shown respect and honour by this ayah, and forgiveness and mercy is promised to them — but their status cannot equal those who declared their Islam despite all apprehensions of extreme hardship.

Ibn Kathir explains the closing words, *"And Allah is All-Aware of what you do"*: He made distinctions between the rewards of the believers who spent and fought before the Conquest and those who did so afterwards — by His knowledge of the **intention** of the former type and their perfect sincerity to Him, all the while spending in times of hardship, poverty and dire straits. In that connection he cites a hadith, without naming the collection it comes from, rendered in our source as: *(Spending one Dirham is preceded over a hundred thousand.)* And there is no doubt, he says, that the people of faith consider **Abū Bakr As-Ṣiddīq** to be the person who has the best share according to the meaning of this ayah: he was the chief of those who implemented it, among all followers of all Prophets, for he spent all of his wealth seeking the Face of Allah — and did it voluntarily, not to repay a debt or a favour that anyone from mankind had on him. May Allah be pleased with him.

## "But to all Allah has promised the best"

The ayah refuses to let ranking curdle into contempt. Those who spent before and after the conquest will all gain a reward for their good deeds, even though some of them vary in rank. Ibn Kathir compares this to 4:95 — Allah has preferred in grades those who strive with their wealth and their lives above those who sit at home, *"Unto each, Allah has promised good."* He also cites a hadith in the Sahih: *(The strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak believer; both have goodness in them.)* The Prophet ﷺ ended his statement that way, Ibn Kathir notes, to draw attention to the second type of believer, so that their own qualities are not forgotten in the midst of preferring the former type. **Preference is not dismissal.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the doctrinal consequence: *al-ḥusnā* — "the good reward" — means that the promise of Paradise and forgiveness extends to **all** the noble Companions, whether they spent and fought before or after the Conquest. **Ibn Ḥazm** says the meaning becomes even clearer when 21:101–102 is appended to it: *"Surely, those for whom the good (news) from Us has come earlier shall be kept far away from it (i.e. from the Hell). They will not hear the slightest of its sound, and they will remain forever in what their selves desire."*

From this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the position of Ahl as-Sunnah wal-Jamāʿah. The Companions are a medium between the Prophet ﷺ and the general body of the Muslim community — without them neither the Qur'an nor its meaning nor the Prophet's ﷺ teachings could reach the Ummah — so their status is recognised in the light of Qur'an and Sunnah, not by historical narrations that are a mixture of right and wrong. If any of them slipped, in most cases it would not exceed a *khataʼ ijtihādī*, an error in considered judgement, rather than a sin or wilful transgression — and by the clear text of a Prophetic Tradition, a *mujtahid* who errs still receives one reward. Imam Ahmad wrote a monograph on the subject, part of which reads: **"It is not lawful for anyone to speak ill of the Companions, or cast aspersions against them, or find fault with them."** Ibn Taymiyyah concluded that he knew of no difference of opinion on the matter: it is imperative to praise them, to seek forgiveness for them, to remember them with compassion, and to hold love and friendship for them. On their mutual disputes, his *Sharḥ al-ʿAqīdah Al-Wāsiṭiyyah* gives the settled position: **they hold their tongues about what happened between the Companions.** This does not mean the Ummah believes every Companion sinless — but their virtues and precedence demand a forgiveness so wide that later members of the Ummah do not have such a scope.

## "Who is he that will lend Allah a handsome loan?" (ayah 11)

After the ranking, an open door: *man dhā alladhī yuqriḍu-llāha qarḍan ḥasanan* — *"Who is he that will lend Allah a handsome loan: then He will increase it manifold to his credit"* — and he will have an honourable reward.

On its scope, **ʿUmar bin Al-Khaṭṭāb** said this ayah refers to spending in Allah's cause; it was also said that it pertains to spending on children. What is correct, Ibn Kathir says, is that it is **more general than that**: all those who spend in the cause of Allah with good intentions and a sincere heart fall under the generality of this ayah. The multiplication is stated elsewhere as *aḍʿāfan kathīrah* — "many times" (2:245) — which Ibn Kathir explains as a handsome reward and tremendous provisions: Paradise on the Day of Resurrection.

**Abū Ad-Daḥdāḥ.** Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded that ʿAbdullāh bin Masʿūd said: when this ayah was revealed, Abū Ad-Daḥdāḥ Al-Anṣārī said, "O Allah's Messenger! Does Allah ask us for a loan?" The Prophet ﷺ said: *(Yes, O Abū Ad-Daḥdāḥ.)* Abū Ad-Daḥdāḥ said, "Verily, I have given my garden as a loan to my Lord." He had a garden that contained six hundred date trees; his wife and children were living in that garden too. He went to his wife and called her, "Umm Ad-Daḥdāḥ!" She said, "Here I am." He said, "Leave the garden, because I have given it as a loan to my Lord, the Exalted and Most Honored." She said: **"That is a successful trade, O Abū Ad-Daḥdāḥ!"** The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *(How plentiful are the sweet date clusters that Abū Ad-Daḥdāḥ has in Paradise!)*

## Living it

The passage ends not on fear but on generosity of judgement: those who gave when giving was costly stand higher — *and to all Allah has promised the best.*

passages.title: Light of believers, darkness of hypocrites
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are a single scene from the Day of Resurrection: a vast, dark gathering-place in which light is handed out, and two crowds — believers and hypocrites — who stood side by side in this world discover that they are no longer in the same place at all. What holds the passage together is one image, light, followed all the way through: it is given (ayah 12), it is begged for and refused (ayah 13), the reason for the refusal is spelled out (ayah 14), and the final sentence is passed (ayah 15).

Ibn Kathir opens his comment on the passage with a single sentence that sets everything up: Allah the Exalted states that the believers **who spend in charity** will come on the Day of Resurrection with their light preceding them in the area of the Gathering, **according to the level of their good deeds**. The light is not an ornament handed out at random. It is measured against a life.

## The darkness before the light

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the passage with a long narration of Sayyidnā Abū Umāmah al-Bāhilī, which Ibn Kathir cites on the authority of Ibn Abī Ḥātim. Abū Umāmah had attended a funeral in Damascus, and when it was over he reminded the people of death, the grave, the Resurrection and the Hereafter. Among his words: people will be transferred from the graves to the plane of gathering, where there will be different stages and places to stand or wait. There comes a stage where, by the divine command, some faces brighten and others are darkened. Then comes a stage where everyone — believers and non-believers alike — is assembled together, **an intense darkness prevails, and nobody is able to see anything.** Only then is light distributed.

That is the setting ayah 12 drops us into, and the whole drama depends on it: the darkness comes first, and it is universal. Whatever light a person has there, he receives there.

Abū Umāmah went on to say that the hypocrites and the infidels would not receive any light, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to the Qur'an's own image for their state — deeds like layers of darkness in a vast deep sea, wave upon wave, cloud above that, "one above the other," so that when a man puts forth his hand he can hardly see it; and the one to whom Allah does not give light can have no light at all (24:40).

## Light measured out by deeds

The clearest picture of what "their light running forward before them" means comes from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, in a report collected by Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Jarīr. He said they will pass over the Ṣirāṭ — the bridge — according to their deeds:

- some will have a light **as large as a mountain**
- some **as a date tree**
- some **as big as a man in the standing position**
- and the least among them has a light **as big as his index finger — lit at times and extinguished at other times.**

Read that last line slowly. A flickering fingertip of light in that darkness is a terrifyingly thin margin — and yet it is light, and its owner is crossing the Ṣirāṭ.

**"and in their right hands."** Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk explained this as their **books of records** — as Allah says elsewhere, "So whosoever is given his record in his right hand" (17:71). So the believer arrives carrying two things: the record and the light.

Then, in ayah 12, the announcement: *Glad tidings for you this Day! Gardens under which rivers flow, to dwell therein forever.* Ibn Kathir notes the phrasing — it will be **said to them**, glad tidings proclaimed to them at that moment, with the permanence stressed: you will remain therein forever. That, and nothing else, is **the great success**.

## Why the hypocrites' light goes out

Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn ʿAbbās — through al-ʿAwfī, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and others — a compact account of ayah 13: when the people are gathering in darkness, Allah will send light; when the believers see the light they will march towards it, and this light will be their guide from Allah to Paradise. When the hypocrites see the believers following the light, **they will follow them.** But Allah will extinguish the light for the hypocrites, and that is when they call out, *"Wait for us! Let us get something from your light."*

Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk adds a detail that changes how the believers appear in this scene. Everyone will be given a light; when they arrive at the Ṣirāṭ the hypocrites' light is extinguished; and when the believers **see** this, they become concerned that their own light will be extinguished too — and that is when they invoke Allah, *"O our Lord! Perfect our light for us."* The believers here are not smug. They are afraid, and they are praying.

**Two reports, and how the scholars reconciled them.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the difference honestly. Abū Umāmah's narration teaches that the infidels and the hypocrites are deprived of light from the very beginning point where it is distributed. But Ṭabarānī reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah will send light to every believer at the bridge, **and also to every hypocrite**, but when the hypocrites reach the bridge their light will be snatched away (cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān from Ibn Kathir). Muslim, Aḥmad and Dāraquṭnī record from Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh that light will at first be given to both believers and hypocrites, and snatched from the hypocrites when they reach the bridge.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān comments that this second version is in keeping with the character of hypocrisy itself: that they should first be shown light and then have it extinguished, leaving them in total darkness, **just as they behaved deceitfully in the world** — as the Qur'an says of the hypocrites, that they try to deceive Allah while He is the One who leaves them in deception (4:142). Imam Baghawī explains the "deception" here to mean that the light will first be sent to them, then snatched away from them **just at the moment they need it most crucially.**

And at that crucial moment, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds (from Mazharī), the believers too will fear that their light might be snatched away, and so they implore: *"Our Lord, perfect for us our light, and forgive us. Indeed You are powerful over everything"* (66:8).

Mazharī reconciles the two versions by distinguishing two kinds of hypocrite. The first appeared in the time of the Prophet ﷺ; they are treated as the disbelievers are, deprived of light from the very outset. The second appeared after his time — and here Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes an important point: they cannot be called *munāfiq* in the true sense of the word, because revelation ended with the departure of the Prophet ﷺ, and **without definitive evidence on the basis of revelation no one can be labelled, identified or classified as a hypocrite.** The *munāfiq* manifests the form of a man of faith in his outward practice while his inner dimension is completely devoid of faith, and there is no way for common people to know this. Allah is fully aware of both dimensions and will treat each one accordingly. These are the ones shown light at first, only to have it put out at the bridge and be left groping in total darkness. Into this category, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, fall those people of this Ummah who distort the Qur'an and Hadith, twisting their meanings to suit their own purposes — "We seek Allah's refuge from it."

## "Go back to your rear" — and the wall

The refusal in ayah 13 is given in the passive: *it will be said.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah, notes that this reply will be given by either **the believers or the angels**. Ibn Kathir's reading of the words is: go back to the dark area you were in, and look for a light **there**.

It is a devastating instruction. What is being asked for cannot be handed over. And as Mazharī describes the hypocrite, his whole outward practice was the form of faith over an inner dimension empty of it — and at this moment the form is exactly what fails.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces what happens next: having received that reply, they return to the place where the light was distributed, **find nothing there**, and try to go back to the believers — but in the meantime the wall is set up between them. They are separated, unable to reach the believers, left in complete darkness, with Allah's mercy on the believers' side and chastisement on theirs.

**What is this wall?** The commentators differ, and the sources report the difference rather than settling it:

- **Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah:** the wall is located between Paradise and Hellfire.
- **ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam:** it is the barrier Allah describes in 7:46, "And between them will be a screen." Ibn Kathir reports the like from Mujāhid and others, and says this **is correct**. Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī also cites Ibn Zayd's view that this wall refers to al-Aʿrāf, a barrier between the believers and the hypocrites, while other commentators hold that the wall is not al-Aʿrāf but some other wall or barrier.

On the **gate** in the wall, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two possibilities: either it is the way through which the believers and the hypocrites will communicate with one another, or it is the door through which all the believers will pass, after which it is sealed off permanently.

Ibn Kathir's gloss on the two faces of the wall is simple and unforgettable: *inside it will be mercy* means Paradise and all that is in it; *outside it will be torment* means the Hellfire — according to Qatādah, Ibn Zayd and others. One structure, mercy on one side of it and fire on the other.

## "Were we not with you?"

Ayah 14 is the most searching moment in the passage, because the hypocrites' complaint is, on its face, **true**. Ibn Kathir spells out what they mean: were we not with you in the life of the world, attending Friday prayers and congregational prayers? Did we not stand with you on Mount ʿArafah during Ḥajj, participate in battle by your side, and perform all types of acts of worship with you?

And the believers answer: **"Yes."** *Balā* — yes, you were with us. The claim is not denied. What follows is the *but*, and it is four charges, one after another:

**1. "You led yourselves into temptations"** — *fatantum anfusakum.* The ruin was self-inflicted.

**2. "You looked forward to destruction"** — *tarabbaṣtum.* Qatādah explains: "Of the truth and its people." Outwardly in the ranks; inwardly waiting for the ranks to break.

**3. "You doubted"** — *irtabtum.* Ibn Kathir specifies the object of the doubt: that Resurrection occurs after death. The very Day they are now standing in is the thing they were unsure of.

**4. "You were deceived by false hopes"** — *gharratkum al-amāniyy.* Ibn Kathir gives two explanations: you said that you would be forgiven your sins; or, as others say, it means this life deceived you.

Then: *till the command of Allah came to pass* — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, **you remained on this path until death came to you.**

And finally: *the deceiver deceived you in regard to Allah* — 'the deceiver' being **Shayṭān**. Qatādah's comment carries real anguish: "They were deceived by ash-Shayṭān. By Allah! They remained deceived until Allah cast them into Hellfire."

Ibn Kathir sums up the believers' whole answer in one line worth memorising: *"You were with us in bodies which were heartless and devoid of intentions."* Present in body, absent in heart and intention — cast in doubt and suspicion, showing off for people, and remembering Allah little. Mujāhid describes the outward closeness in the world: the hypocrites were with the believers in this life, marrying from among each other, yet betraying them even when they were associating with them — "They were dead." Both, he says, will be given a light on the Day of Resurrection, but the light of the hypocrites will be extinguished when they reach the wall, and **that is when the two camps separate and part.**

## Ayah 15: no ransom

The verdict has three parts. **No ransom** shall be taken on that Day — not from the hypocrites addressed, nor from those who disbelieved.

**"Your abode is the Fire"** — Ibn Kathir: the Fire is your final destination, and to it will be your return for residence.

**"That is your protector."** Ibn Kathir's gloss makes the sentence land: it is **the worthy shelter for you rather than any other residence, because of your disbelief and your doubt** — and how evil is the Fire as a final destination. The only shelter left is the one thing no one would shelter in.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a note on the shape of the whole scene. In the matter of light, **the infidels are not mentioned anywhere**, because in their case there is no question of having such a light. The hypocrites are mentioned, and there are the two narrations already seen: either they receive no light at all from the outset, or they receive it at first and it is extinguished when they arrive at the Bridge of Ṣirāṭ, with a wall erected as a barrier between them and the believers. This goes to show, it says, that only the believers will cross the Bridge of Ṣirāṭ over Hell; the infidels and pagans will not pass over the Bridge at all but be pushed straight into the Fire through the doors of Hell. Sinful believers, who are kept in the Fire for a while to be cleansed of their sins, will fall while crossing the Bridge; the rest of the believers will cross safely and enter Paradise — as explicitly stated by Shāh ʿAbdul-Qādir Dehlawī and supported by *Durr*. And Allah knows best.

## What actually earns light

Since light on that Day is proportioned to deeds, the obvious question is: what produces it? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, following Tafsīr Mazharī, gathers exactly this list from Qur'an and Hadith — offered, in its own words, in the hope that Allah will grant us light. A selection:

- **Walking to the mosque in the dark.** "Give glad tidings to those who go to the mosque in the darkness of night that they will receive perfect light on the Day of Judgment." (Reported by Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi from Buraidah, and Ibn Majah from Anas — and reported also by a long list of other Companions.)
- **Guarding the five prayers.** He who takes care of his five daily prayers, they will serve as light, proof and salvation for him on the Day of Judgment; he who fails to take care of them will have no light, no proof and no salvation, and will be in the company of Qārūn, Hāmān and Firʿawn. (Reported by Aḥmad and Ṭabarānī from Ibn ʿUmar.)
- **Sūrah al-Kahf.** Whoever recites it will have so much light on the Day of Judgment that it will spread from his place to Makkah; in another narration, whoever recites it on a Friday will have light extending from his feet to the heights of the heaven. (Reported by Ṭabarānī from Abū Saʿīd.)
- **Even a single verse** of the Qur'an recited will be a light for him on that Day. (Reported by Aḥmad from Abū Hurayrah.)
- **Sending ṣalāh upon the Prophet ﷺ** shall be a cause of light on the Bridge of Ṣirāṭ. (Reported by Daylamī from Abū Hurayrah.)
- **Ḥajj:** the hair that falls at the time of shaving when coming out of iḥrām will be a light on that Day (Ṭabarānī from ʿUbādah ibn Ṣāmit); and stoning the jamarāt at Minā will be a light on that Day (Musnad of Bazzār from Ibn Masʿūd).
- **Hair turning grey in Islam** will be a light for him on the Day of Judgment. (Ṭabarānī, with a good chain, from Abū Hurayrah.)
- **Shooting even one arrow in Allah's way** while fighting in jihad will be a light for him on that Day. (Bazzār, with a good chain, from Abū Hurayrah.)
- **Relieving another Muslim's calamity:** Allah will create for him two compartments of light at the bridge, which will brighten up a whole world. (Ṭabarānī from Abū Hurayrah.)

And the counterweight, on the darkness side: "Beware of *ẓulm* (injustice), because that will yield *ẓulumāt* — layers of darkness — on the Day of Judgment." (Bukhari and Muslim from Ibn ʿUmar, Muslim from Jābir, Ḥākim from Abū Hurayrah and Ibn ʿUmar, and Ṭabarānī from Ibn Ziyād.) The two words in the Arabic come from one root: the wrong itself is what turns into that darkness.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is clear that no one can be labelled a hypocrite without definitive evidence from revelation, and that revelation ended with the Prophet ﷺ. So the question these ayat leave is not a question about anyone else. It is this: when the lights go out and every outward form is stripped away, **what will still be burning?**

Notice where the light in these narrations comes from. Not from grand public achievements, but from a walk to the mosque in the darkness of night; a prayer guarded when it would have been easy to let it slip; a single verse recited; a ṣalāh sent on the Prophet ﷺ; a calamity lifted off another Muslim. Set that beside Ibn Kathir's description of the other party — bodies without hearts or intentions, showing off for people, remembering Allah little — and the contrast is exact. These are deeds with no audience.

And keep the believers' prayer close. Seeing the light go out beside them, they do not congratulate themselves; they call on Allah: *"Our Lord, perfect for us our light, and forgive us. Indeed You are powerful over everything."* If the ones carrying the light pray that, so should we.

passages.title: Has the time not come for humbled hearts
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are one movement: a tender rebuke to believers whose hearts had begun to cool (16), a promise that Allah revives a dead heart as He revives dead ground (17), the way back — open-handed giving lent to Allah Himself (18) — and the honour He confers on those who truly believe (19).

## "Has the time not yet come…" — a question that is really a summons

Ayah 16 does not command. It asks. *Has the time not yet come for the believers that their hearts should be humble for the remembrance of Allah and for the truth that has descended?* Ibn Kathir unfolds it: has the moment not arrived for the believers to feel humility in their hearts through the remembrance of Allah, through hearing subtle advice, through the recitation of the Qur'an — so that they comprehend the Qur'an, abide by it, and hear and obey?

Notice who is addressed: people who already have faith. They are not being told to believe; they are being told that believing was supposed to *do* something to them by now, and it has not.

**The occasions of revelation.** Muslim recorded that 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud said: "Only four years separated our acceptance of Islam and the revelation of this Ayah, in which Allah subtly admonished us" — and he then recited the words of ayah 16. Ibn Kathir notes that this is the narration Muslim collected, just before the end of his book, and that An-Nasa'i also collected it in the tafsir of this ayah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same report from Ibn Mas'ud, and describes what it administered as a *mild* reproof, not a condemnation.

Ibn 'Abbas reports the cause: some of the believers were found to be lacking in firmness, and a certain laziness was felt in their practice — and so this ayah was revealed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that Ibn 'Abbas's narration also carries a further piece of information, recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim: that this admonitory ayah was revealed thirteen years after revelation had started.

Imam A'mash offered a third angle, cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān from Ruh al-Maʿani: after settling in Madinah the Companions experienced socio-economic comfort and prosperity, and as a result some of them relaxed in the effort they used to pour into good works. The rebuke is aimed at that slackening — the kind that arrives not with persecution but with ease.

The reports differ on the count of years. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets them side by side and closes: *Allah knows best.*

## What *khushuʿ* actually is

Everything in ayah 16 turns on one word: **khushūʿ**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, quoting Ibn Kathir, gives the sense of *khushūʿ al-qalb* — humility of the heart — as: for the heart to soften; to be receptive to advice; to be obedient; to submit. Not one of them is a feeling that comes and goes.

Ruh al-Maʿani, as quoted in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, sharpens it for the Qur'anic context: khushūʿ means a complete willingness to yield to the divine injunctions — to what Allah commands and what He forbids — without allowing any laxity in following them. So this is not a mood, not a moist eye during recitation that leaves the rest of the week untouched. It is a settled readiness of the heart to be told what to do by Allah and to do it.

And it is not decoration on the religion — it is the hinge. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states that all actions revolve around khushūʿ al-qalb, and cites the narration of Shaddad ibn Aws that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The first thing that will be taken away from the people will be their humility or humbleness [khushūʿ]." (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits this through Ibn Kathir without naming a collection.) Before outward religion collapses, the inward softness quietly leaves.

Note too *what* the heart is humbled toward. Ayah 16 names two things: **the remembrance of Allah** and **the truth that has descended** — the revelation itself. Humility before Allah and humility before His Book are not two projects.

## The warning: the long stretch of time

The second half of ayah 16 gives the reason for urgency: *lest they become as those who received the Scripture before, and the term was prolonged for them and so their hearts were hardened, and many of them were rebellious.*

Ibn Kathir reads this as an outright prohibition: Allah forbids the believers to imitate those given the Scriptures before them, the Jews and Christians. He traces how the hardening happened — as time passed they changed the Book of Allah they possessed and sold it for a small, miserable price; they abandoned it behind their backs; they were impressed and consumed by various opinions and false creeds; they made their rabbis and priests into gods beside Allah. The consequence: their hearts became hard, they would not accept advice, and their hearts did not feel humbled by Allah's promises or His threats.

The phrase *the term was prolonged for them* is the quiet centre of the warning. No single catastrophic sin is named. Time simply stretched out between them and the moment of revelation, and in that stretch the heart calcified. This is a warning about drift — what happens to a religion inherited rather than encountered.

Ibn Kathir brings a parallel ayah: *So, because of their breach of their covenant, We cursed them and made their hearts grow hard. They changed the words from their right places and have abandoned a good part of the Message that was sent to them* (5:13). He explains that their hearts became corrupt and hardened, and out of that they acquired the behaviour of changing Allah's Speech from its appropriate places and meanings, abandoning the acts of worship they were commanded to perform and committing what they were prohibited to do. This, he says, is precisely why Allah forbade the believers from imitating them **in any way, be it basic or detailed matters**.

And *many of them were rebellious* — Ibn Kathir explains this as rebellion *in action*: their hearts are corrupt and therefore their actions are invalid.

## Ayah 17: the mercy hidden inside the rebuke

*Know that Allah gives life to the earth after its death! Indeed We have made clear the Ayat to you, if you but understand.*

Ibn Kathir's reading is the key to the whole passage. This ayah, he says, indicates that Allah brings subtleness to hearts after they have become hard, guides the confused after they were led astray, and relieves hardships after they have intensified. Just as He brings life back to the dead and dry earth by sending the needed abundant rain, He also guides hardened hearts with the proofs and evidences of the Qur'an — and the light of faith gains access to hearts once again, after they were closed and, as a consequence, no guidance was able to reach them.

The sequence is merciful. Ayah 16 diagnoses a hardening heart; ayah 17 immediately says the hardening is not a life sentence. Dead ground looks finished and is not. The rain for the heart is the Qur'an.

Ibn Kathir ends with praise to the One who guides whomever He wills after they were misguided, and who misguides those who were led aright before — for surely it is He who does what He wills, and He is the All-Wise, the Most Just in all that He does, the Most Subtle, the Most Aware, the Most High, the Proud. The traffic runs both ways, which is why ayah 16's question is urgent and not merely poignant. *If you but understand* — the ayat have been made clear; what remains is the use we make of our own reason.

## Ayah 18: giving as the proof of a softened heart

Having asked for the heart, Allah now names the deed that shows the heart has answered: *Verily, those who give Sadaqat, men and women, and lend Allah a handsome loan — it shall be increased manifold for them, and theirs shall be an honourable reward.*

*Sadaqat* is the plural of *sadaqah*: voluntary charitable giving, wealth handed over for the sake of Allah. Ibn Kathir notes that Allah is describing here the reward He will award to those who spend from their wealth — **whether male or female**, says the ayah explicitly — upon the needy, the poor and the meek.

**"Lend Allah a handsome loan."** Ibn Kathir defines the *handsome* quality of the loan not by its size but by its motive: they give in charity with a good heart seeking the pleasure of Allah, and they do not seek worldly rewards or appreciation from those to whom they give. And notice the word Allah chooses: a *loan*. The Owner of everything, who needs nothing, calls your charity a loan to Him.

**"It shall be increased manifold."** Ibn Kathir explains that Allah will multiply these good deeds from tenfold, up to seven hundredfold and even more than that. **"And theirs shall be an honourable reward"** — a generous, handsome reward, a good dwelling to return to, and an honourable final destination.

A hard heart grips its wealth; a soft heart lets it go. Charity is khushūʿ made visible.

## Ayah 19: who exactly are the ṣiddīqūn?

*And those who believe in Allah and His Messengers — they are the Ṣiddīqūn, and the martyrs with their Lord. They shall have their reward and their light. But those who disbelieve and deny Our Ayat — they shall be the dwellers of the blazing Fire.*

A *ṣiddīq* is a true believer of the highest calibre — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "the most righteous". A *shahīd* (plural *shuhadāʾ*) is a martyr, and the word also carries the sense of one who bears witness — both senses are alive in the discussion below. The scholars genuinely differed over how to read this sentence.

**First view: two groups, read as separate sentences.** Ibn Kathir notes that Al-'Awfi reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning of *they are the Ṣiddīqūn* does **not** continue into what follows — so "and the martyrs are with their Lord" begins a new statement. Abu Ad-Duha would stop his recitation at *they are the Ṣiddīqūn* and then begin afresh with *and the martyrs are with their Lord*; Masruq, Ad-Dahhak, Muqatil bin Hayyan and others said similarly.

Al-A'mash narrated from Abu Ad-Duha from Masruq from 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud that "they are of three categories" — meaning those who spend in charity (ayah 18), the ṣiddīqūn, and the martyrs.

Ibn Kathir supports the distinction with 4:69: *And whoso obey Allah and the Messenger, then they will be in the company of those on whom Allah has bestowed His grace, of the Prophets, the Ṣiddīqīn, the martyrs, and the righteous.* Since Allah there made a distinction between the ṣiddīqīn and the martyrs, they are two distinct categories — and Ibn Kathir concludes that there is no doubt the status of ṣiddīq is better than that of the martyr.

**Second view: every true believer shares in both titles.** Read plainly, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, this ayah indicates that every believer is a ṣiddīq and a shahīd — and on the basis of it Qatadah and 'Amr ibn Maimun maintained exactly that. Ibn Jarir reports that Bara' ibn 'Azib narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "The believers of my Ummah are all shuhadāʾ" — and in support he recited this very ayah. Ibn Abi Hatim reports that Abu Hurayrah, with some of the Companions gathered around him one day, said: "Each one of you is a ṣiddīq and a shahīd." This startled them and they exclaimed, "What are you saying, Abu Hurayrah?" He replied: if you do not believe me, then read this ayah.

**How the two are reconciled.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises 4:69 as the difficulty — if the Prophets, ṣiddīqīn, shuhadāʾ and righteous are listed separately, the three categories would appear to be genuinely different; otherwise there would have been no need to mention them separately. So some scholars hold that the ṣiddīqīn and shuhadāʾ in the strict sense are the highest and most sublime categories, and that ayah 19 calls all believers by those names in the sense that every believer is included in those groups *in some degree*. Ruh al-Maʿani adds a caution: it is appropriate to take ayah 19 as referring to people who have perfect faith and perform deeds of righteousness — since believers who indulge in deeds not in keeping with the dictates of their faith can hardly be called ṣiddīq or shahīd.

That caution is reinforced by the reported words of the Prophet ﷺ that the cursers cannot be shuhadāʾ (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives this without naming a collection). And by a scene from 'Umar al-Faruq: he asked people what was the matter with them, that they see someone defaming people and neither stop him nor raise an eyebrow. They replied that they feared his violent tongue. 'Umar answered that if that is the case, they cannot be shuhadāʾ. Ibn Athir cited this narration and explained that it means such timid people will not be among the *witnesses* who will bear witness against the communities of the previous Prophets.

**A third position.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also records Mazhari's view that "those who believe" in ayah 19 refers only to the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ — those who believed in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, saw him, and had the pleasure of his company — so that the restrictive phrase *it is they who are the ṣiddīqūn* indicates that the rank of ṣiddīq is limited to them. Mujaddid Alf Thani states that all the noble Companions had a share in the noble qualities of prophethood, such that any Companion who saw the Prophet ﷺ in a state of faith even for a short time is absorbed and drowned in such qualities of perfection. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān leaves it with: *Allah, the Pure and Exalted, knows best!*

**"Their reward and their light."** Ibn Kathir explains that Allah will grant them a generous reward and a tremendous light that will precede before them — and that in this the believers vary in the level of reward they receive, according to their good actions in the life of this world. That the martyrs are "with their Lord" means, he says, that they will be in the gardens of Paradise, and he cites what is recorded in the Sahih: the souls of the martyrs live in the bodies of green birds, which fly wherever they wish in Paradise and then return to their nests in chandeliers; once their Lord cast a glance at them and asked, "Do you want anything?" They said, "We wish that You return us to the life of the world, so that we may fight in Your cause and be killed as we were killed the first time." Allah said, "I have decreed that they shall not be returned to it again."

Even martyrdom has ranks. Imam Ahmad recorded that 'Umar bin Al-Khattab said he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say there are four ranks of martyrs. The first: a man who believes and is true in faith, who meets the enemy in battle, fulfils his duty to Allah and is killed — and here the Prophet ﷺ raised his head until his cap fell off, and the same happened to 'Umar, showing how far others must look up to see him. The second: a believer who meets the enemy and is struck by a stray arrow which causes him to die. The third: a believer who has combined good deeds with evil deeds, who meets the enemy and is truthful to his duty to Allah until he is killed. And the fourth: a believer who has committed sins excessively, who meets the enemy and is truthful to his duty to Allah and is killed. Of this report, 'Ali bin Al-Madini said, "This Egyptian chain is *Salih*, useful," and At-Tirmidhi said, "*Hasan Gharib*."

Ibn Kathir also brings, from Imam Malik bin Anas's Muwatta', the report of Abu Sa'id Al-Khudri that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said the people of Paradise will look at the dwellers of the lofty mansions as one looks at a brilliant star far away in the east or in the west on the horizon, because of their superiority over one another. The people asked, "O Allah's Messenger! Are these lofty mansions for the Prophets whom none else can reach?" He ﷺ replied: *"No! By Him in Whose Hand is my soul — these are for men who believe in Allah and believe in the Messengers."* Al-Bukhari and Muslim also collected this hadith. That is exactly the description of ayah 19: the highest stations are opened by faith itself.

The passage ends with the two destinations set side by side: *But those who disbelieve and deny Our Ayat — they shall be the dwellers of the blazing Fire.* Ibn Kathir observes that this mentions the destination and the condition of the miserable ones, after Allah mentioned the destination and rewards of the happy ones.

## Living it

- **Take the question personally.** If four years was long enough for Allah to ask it of Ibn Mas'ud's generation, no length of time in Islam makes anyone exempt.
- **Watch for the comfort-drift.** A'mash located the slackening precisely where life got easier — comfort and prosperity in Madinah, and effort in good works quietly relaxing.
- **Give the Qur'an access.** Ayah 17 says the hardened heart is guided by the proofs and evidences of the Qur'an as dead ground is revived by rain — so sitting under real recitation and real advice is the mechanism, not an optional extra.
- **Test the heart with the wallet.** Ayah 18 makes charity the visible proof, and Ibn Kathir sets its standard: given with a good heart seeking the pleasure of Allah, with no appetite for worldly return and none even for the recipient's appreciation.
- **Do not despair of a hard heart.** The order of ayat 16 and 17 is itself the consolation: the One asking the question is the One who revives what has died.

passages.title: A withering world and a decree already written
passages.tafsir:
Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the thread that binds these five ayat: there are two sets of factors that make a person unmindful of Allah and the Hereafter — over-involvement in the wealth, comfort and luxuries of this world, and the calamities and hardships that leave a person hopeless. Ayat 20–21 answer the first, ayat 22–24 the second, and the hinge between them is that everything was written before it was brought into being. Maʿārif also notes why the passage comes here: the preceding verses described the people of Paradise and the inhabitants of Hell, so Allah now shows what the life that costs people the Hereafter actually is.

## Ayah 20: five words that map a whole lifetime

Allah does not merely say this life is small. He lists it: **laʿib** (play), **lahw** (amusement), **zīnah** (show of beauty), **tafākhur** (exchange of boastful claims), **takāthur** (competition to increase in riches and children).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a striking observation: they are listed in *the same order in which they occur* in a human life.

- **Laʿib** is play with no purpose at all — like the movements of little children.
- **Lahw** is a game or sport meant initially for enjoyment, but which may serve some secondary purpose such as physical exercise: ball games, swimming, target-shooting. Maʿārif notes that Prophetic Traditions have termed swimming and target-shooting as good sports. This is the stage of the bigger children.
- **Zīnah** comes with youth, when a person wants to adorn his body and his dress and to show their beauty.
- **Tafākhur** follows: the urge to prove one's superiority over one's mates and to make boastful claims.
- **Takāthur** belongs to old age: the keen competition and rivalry to amass wealth and multiply children — power, prestige, pride and position becoming a man's capital goods and investments.

The insight that gives the list its force: while a person is inside a phase, he feels satisfied with it and regards it as the goal of his life — snatch a toy from a child and he grieves exactly as a grown man grieves over his valuable wealth and property being seized. Once the phase is over he realises its absurdity and hollowness, and takes to the next phase. The Qurʼan reminds him that this phase too will pass away. The next stage is *barzakh* — the grave — followed by the Day of Resurrection, and Maʿārif says a person needs to think about those stages, because they are the ones that are truly eternal, without an end.

Ibn Kathir reads the list as Allah "degrading the significance of this life and belittling it" — this is what it amounts to *for its people* — and connects it to Sūrah Āl ʿImrān: "Beautified for men is the love of things they covet; women, children, much of gold and silver, branded beautiful horses, cattle and well-tilled land. This is the pleasure of the present world's life; but Allah has the excellent return with Him" (3:14).

## The rain that becomes straw

**Ghayth** is the word for rain. Ibn Kathir explains it as the rain that comes down to mankind *after they had felt despair*, citing "And He it is Who sends down the Ghayth after they have despaired" (42:28). The parable begins not with ordinary rain but with rescue. That is how the world presents itself.

**"The growth is pleasing to the kuffār."** Here the commentators divide, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays the disagreement out fairly. *Kuffār* is the plural of *kāfir*, generally used as the opposite of *muʼminīn* and so meaning non-believers — but its literal sense also carries the meaning of **farmers**. Some scholars take it in that literal sense: farmers are happy to see the vegetation that grows in the aftermath of rain. Other commentators keep the popular sense: it is the non-believers who are attracted by the greenery.

The objection to the second view is obvious — believers admire lush vegetation too. Maʿārif gives the commentators' answer: a believer's pleasure is directed towards Allah; he believes everything is the outcome of Allah's power, wisdom and mercy. He does not make it the goal of his life, and he gives up the cherished and precious things of this mortal world in consideration for the higher, eternal things of the Hereafter. So any believer who fulfils the requirements of his faith is not attracted even by the greatest wealth of this world as a *kāfir* is — which is why the attraction is attributed to the non-believer.

Then the three verbs of collapse: **yahīj** (it dries up), **musfarran** (you see it turning yellow), **ḥuṭām** (it becomes straw, scattered pieces of dust). Ibn Kathir applies this to a human being: young and strong in the beginning, youthful and handsome; then slowly growing older, manners changing and strength weakening; then old and feeble, when moving becomes difficult and easy things pass beyond his ability. He recites over it: "Allah is He Who created you in a state of weakness, then gave you strength after weakness, then after strength gave you weakness and grey hair" (30:54).

## Two things waiting on the other side

Ibn Kathir: the parable indicates the near demise of this life and the imminent end of it, while in contrast the Hereafter is surely coming — so those who hear it should be aware of the significance of the Hereafter and feel eagerness for the goodness it contains.

And in the Hereafter there are exactly two things: **severe torment**, or **forgiveness from Allah and His pleasure (riḍwān)**. Maʿārif notes that punishment is mentioned first, because the preceding verses described people over-absorbed in worldly pleasures, whose outcome is precisely that chastisement. It also notes something in the pairing given to believers: forgiveness of sins is already a boon, since it saves one from punishment — but beyond being saved, he will attain Paradise and its eternal favours, and that is the manifestation of divine pleasure.

**"And the life of this world is only a deceiving enjoyment"** — *matāʿ al-ghurūr*. Ibn Kathir: an enjoyment that deceives those who incline to it. Those who recline into it will admire it and hold it dear, so much so that they might think this is the only life, with no life or dwelling after it — while in reality it is insignificant as compared to the Hereafter. Maʿārif puts it plainly: it is not a capital that may be useful in odd times. Only one conclusion remains for a reasonable man — do not be over-involved in it, and be eager to obtain the bounties of the Hereafter.

## Ayah 21: race

The verb is **sābiqū** — not merely walk, but *compete*, race one another. Ibn Kathir places a hadith right before this command. Imam Ahmad recorded that ʿAbdullah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"Paradise is nearer to any of you than the strap on his shoe, and so is the Fire."** Al-Bukhari collected this hadith through the narration of Ath-Thawri. Ibn Kathir explains: this indicates the close proximity of both good and evil in relation to mankind. And because that is the case, Allah encouraged mankind to rush to acts of righteousness and obedience and to avoid the prohibitions — so that their sins and errors are forgiven and they acquire rewards and an exalted status.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two possible senses of the race:

1. **Race against yourself.** No one has a guarantee for the continuance of his life, health and strength. One should not put off righteous deeds to a future that illness, inability or even death may never let him reach. You are racing to accumulate the treasure of good deeds *before* such inabilities arrive and stop you.
2. **Race with one another.** From the early generations, cited via *Rūḥ*: Sayyidunā ʿAlī advises, "Be among the first ones to go to the mosque and the last ones to come out." Sayyidunā ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿūd advises, "Go forward to be in the first line of jihad." Sayyidunā Anas states, "Try to be present for the first takbīr of the congregational prayer."

**How wide is Paradise?** "As the width of the heaven and the earth." Maʿārif notes a fine point: the parallel verse in Āl ʿImrān has *samāwāt* (heavens, plural) — "And march forth in the way to forgiveness from your Lord, and for Paradise as wide as the heavens and the earth, prepared for those who have taqwā" (3:133) — while here *samāʼ* is singular. Both, it explains, refer to all seven heavens: put the vastness of the seven heavens and the earth together, and that is the *width* of Paradise. Since the length of a thing is normally greater than its breadth, its length is greater still — though the word "width" is sometimes used simply in the general sense of vastness. In either case the purport is the same: Paradise is so vast that it can accommodate the entire heavens and the earth in its vastness. Ibn Kathir notes the difference in qualification too: there, prepared for the people of taqwā; here, "prepared for those who believe in Allah and His Messengers."

## "That is the grace of Allah"

A command to race could easily be misread as: Paradise is the wage your deeds have earned. The closing words of ayah 21 forbid that reading. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the point explicitly — good actions are not necessarily the sufficient cause for attaining Paradise. A man's life-long actions cannot be an adequate price even for the bounties he has already received *in this world*, let alone the everlasting bounties of Paradise. Anyone who enters will do so out of Allah's grace and mercy. It cites a Prophetic hadith recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥain on the authority of Sayyidunā Abū Hurairah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "No one will attain salvation by means of his actions only." The Companions asked, "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He replied, "No, not even I will attain Paradise because of my actions, unless Allah bestows His grace and compassion on me."

Ibn Kathir illustrates the same phrase with the story of the poor emigrants, from a hadith he notes is collected in the Ṣaḥīḥ. They came to the Messenger ﷺ saying, "O Allah's Messenger! The wealthy people will get higher grades and permanent enjoyment." He asked, "Why is that?" They said: they pray as we pray and fast as we fast, but they give in charity whereas we cannot, and they free servants whereas we cannot afford it. He ﷺ said: **"Shall I tell you of a good deed that, if you acted upon, you would catch up with those who have surpassed you? None would overtake you and be better than you, except those who might do the same. Say 'Glorious is Allah,' 'Allah is Most Great,' and 'Praise be to Allah,' thirty-three times each after every prayer."** Later they came back and said, "Our wealthy brethren heard what we did and they started doing the same." And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ answered with the very words of the ayah: **"This is the favour of Allah that He gives to whom He wills."**

It was never a wage — it is His favour, given to whom He wills.

## Ayah 22: written before it was made

Now the passage turns to hardship. **"No calamity occurs on the earth nor in yourselves but it is inscribed in a Book before We bring it into existence."**
