Ibn Kathir reads "no calamity occurs on the earth nor in yourselves" as: there is nothing that touches you or happens in existence — and "before We bring it into existence" as: before We created the creation and started life. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies the Book as the *Lawḥ Maḥfūẓ*, the Preserved Tablet, and spells the two halves out concretely — calamity *in the earth* covers famine, earthquake, destruction of crops, loss in business, loss of wealth and property, and the loss of friends and loved ones; calamity *in yourselves* covers illnesses of all sorts, and all kinds of wounds, hurt and injury. Qatādah gives the same division in brief: on the earth, famine; in yourselves, suffering and diseases.

Qatādah adds a sobering word: "We were told that every person who suffers a prick of a thorn, a twisted ankle, or a bleeding vein, has it occur on account of his sins. What Allah forgives is even more." The consolation is in that last clause — whatever is being answered for by these small wounds, far more is being simply pardoned.

Ibn Kathir states that this great, honourable ayah provides clear evidence against the misguidance of the Qadariyyah sect, who deny Allah's pre-ordainment and His knowledge of everything before it occurs.

He then cites the hadith that dates the writing. Imam Ahmad recorded that ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr bin al-ʿĀṣ said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say, **'Allah ordained the measures of everything fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth.'**" Muslim collected this hadith in his Ṣaḥīḥ with the addition, **"And His Throne was over the water."** At-Tirmidhi also collected it and said, "Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ."

**"Verily, that is easy for Allah."** Ibn Kathir: He knows all things before they occur, and He records them exactly as they will occur when they occur — and this is easy for Him. Allah knows what happened, what will happen, what did *not* happen, and what shape and form it would have taken if it were to happen.

## Ayah 23: the purpose of knowing

Ayah 23 opens with a purpose clause — *li-kaylā*, "so that you may not" — telling you why ayah 22 was told to you at all.

Ibn Kathir paraphrases: We informed you of Our encompassing knowledge, recording all things before they occur and creating all things in due measure known to Us, **so that you may know that what has met you would never have missed you, and what has missed you would never have met you.** Therefore do not grieve for what you have missed of fortune — had it been destined for you, you would have achieved it. Maʿārif adds the other side of the same purpose: nor should we over-exult in the comforts or wealth we enjoy here and in turn become neglectful about Allah and the Hereafter.

A point of recitation: the phrase is also recited *bimā atākum*, "over that which came to you," alongside *bimā ātākum*, "that which has been given to you." Ibn Kathir notes that both meanings are related.

Then the other half. In Ibn Kathir's paraphrase: do not boast before people about what Allah has favoured you with, because it is not you who earned it by your efforts — all this came your way because Allah destined it for you and provided it for you. Do not use what Allah has granted you as a reason to boast and become arrogant with others. Hence **"And Allah does not love every self-admiring boaster"** — *mukhtāl fakhūr*, the one who acts arrogantly with other people.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notices the wording. "Does not love" in fact implies that Allah *hates* those who become proud of the bounties they enjoy in this world. Why the softer phrase, then? Maʿārif suggests it is perhaps an indication that an intelligent person should consider, about all his actions, **whether or not the act he intends is dear to Allah**.

Two sayings from the early authorities put this into practice. ʿIkrimah said: "Everyone of us feels happiness and grief. However, make your joy with gratitude and endure your grief with patience." And Sayyidunā ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbās — in a report Maʿārif attributes to Ḥākim, who rates it ṣaḥīḥ (see *Rūḥ*) — said that it is a man's natural disposition that certain things cheer him up and others make him miserable, whereas the right position is this: when misery befalls him he should endure it with patience and earn reward in the Hereafter, and when he experiences joy he should receive it with gratitude to Allah and earn reward in the Hereafter.

The ayah does not forbid feeling; it redirects it. Grief becomes ṣabr, joy becomes shukr, and both become reward in the Hereafter.

## Ayah 24: the miser and the self-sufficient Lord

Ayah 24 identifies the boaster of ayah 23 by his conduct: **"those who are misers and enjoin miserliness upon people."** Ibn Kathir's comment is short and severe — they commit evil and encourage people to commit it. The two ayat belong together: a man who believes his wealth is his own achievement (ayah 23) will naturally hoard it and urge others to hoard (ayah 24).

**"And whoever turns away"** — Ibn Kathir: from abiding by Allah's commandments and obeying Him — **"then Allah is al-Ghanī, al-Ḥamīd,"** the Rich, Worthy of all praise. Ibn Kathir sets beside it the words of Mūsā, peace be upon him: "If you disbelieve, you and all on earth together, then verily, Allah is Rich, Owner of all praise" (14:8). Turning away leaves Allah exactly as He is — free of all need, and worthy of all praise.

## Holding the passage together

**When life is green and pleasing** (ayah 20), remember it is a crop that will yellow into straw — and race instead for a Garden as wide as the heavens and the earth (ayah 21), knowing the Garden itself is His grace, not your wage. **When life strikes you** (ayah 22), remember it was in the Book before it was brought into being, so that grief over what escaped you does not overwhelm you (ayah 23). **In both states, watch your hands**: do not boast over gifts, do not clutch them, do not urge others to clutch (ayat 23–24).

The hadith of the shoe strap is the sentence to carry away. Good and evil are both that close; which is exactly why Allah tells you to run.

passages.title: Why messengers came and how nations answered
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These three ayat answer one question: **why did Allah send messengers, and what happened when He did?** Ayah 25 gives the purpose — clear proofs, a Book, and a Balance, "so that people may uphold justice." Ayat 26 and 27 trace the record: Nuh, Ibrahim, the chain of prophets in their descendants, and finally 'Isa (peace be upon them all) — and after each sending, the same refrain: *many of them are rebellious*.

## Ayah 25: three things sent down

**"Clear proofs" (al-bayyinat).** Ibn Kathir explains these as "the miracles, the unequivocal evidences and the plain proofs." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *bayyinat* literally means clear or evident things and could also mean clear injunctions — but since the Book is mentioned separately right after, the stronger reading is that *bayyinat* means the miracles and proofs of prophethood while **the Book** sets out the injunctions in detail.

**"And the Mizan" — the Balance.** Ibn Kathir reports from Mujahid, Qatadah and others that the Mizan here means **justice** — the truth "attested to by the sound, straight minds that oppose misguided opinions and ideas," the instinct the Qur'an calls the *fitrah*, "Allah's Fitra with which He has created mankind" (30:30), and the same balance Allah set up alongside the heavens (55:7). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word further: *mizan* originally names an instrument of weighing, and beyond the ordinary scale every instrument devised to weigh and measure other things — even those that measure light or wind — falls under this category.

**How does a Balance "come down"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the commentators' answers:

- *Ruh ul-Maʿani*, *Mazhari* and others: what came down is the **divine law governing the use of the Balance and the administration of justice** — the rules, not the object.
- *Qurtubi*: only the Book was literally sent down; the Balance is joined to the same verb while carrying the sense of *inventing and placing*, a common Arabic usage. The full sense: *We sent down the Book and We placed the Scale* — the wording of 55:7, "And He raised the sky high, and placed the scale."
- Some traditions relate that a balance was actually sent down from the heavens to Nuh (peace be upon him), who was enjoined to weigh with it and fulfil people's rights — reported with the reservation, "Allah knows best."

**"So that people may uphold justice" (li-yaqūma al-nāsu bi'l-qist).** This is the stated purpose of prophecy itself. Ibn Kathir defines that justice as "truth and fairness that is found in the obedience of the Messengers, in all that they conveyed from their Lord, and following all they commanded" — so *qist* here is not merely courtroom fairness; it is life ordered by revelation. What the prophets brought is true in what it conveys, just in all its orders and prohibitions: "And the Word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and in justice" (6:115). Ibn Kathir carries the line to Paradise, where the believers say, "Indeed, the Messengers of our Lord did come with the truth" (7:43).

## Iron: the last instrument, not the first

**"And We sent down iron, wherein is mighty power, as well as many benefits for mankind."**

*Mighty power* — Ibn Kathir: "We made iron a deterrent for those who refuse the truth and oppose it **after the proof has been established against them**." He points to the shape of the Prophet's ﷺ own mission: thirteen years in Makkah, arguing against the idolaters and explaining *tawhid* with detail and proofs. Only once the evidence was established against those who defied him did Allah decree the Hijrah — and then came the order to fight.

Here Ibn Kathir cites **Imam Ahmad and Abu Dawud**, who recorded that 'Abdullah bin 'Umar said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *I was sent with the sword just before the Hour so that Allah be worshipped alone without partners. My provision was placed under the shadow of my spear, and those who defy my order were disgraced and humiliated, and he who imitates a people is one of them.*

Hence, Ibn Kathir continues, "mighty power" is said in reference to weapons — swords, spears, daggers, arrows, shields and the like.

*Benefits for mankind* — and here his list is deliberately domestic: coins, hammers, axes, saws, chisels, shovels, and the tools people use for tilling the land, sowing, cooking and making dough. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point for a later age: there is some iron in almost everything man invents.

**Why "sent down" for something mined from the ground?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: *anzala* here stands for *khalaqa* ("He created"), as in "He sent down to you of the cattle eight couples" (39:6). The wording signals, says *Ruh ul-Maʿani*, that everything existing in this world was recorded in the Preserved Tablet long before it came into existence.

**The sequence is the lesson.** The Book sets forth the rights of Allah and of human beings and prohibits violating them; the Balance lays down the system that maintains just equilibrium in human social relations; both aim at *li-yaqūma al-nāsu bi'l-qist*. **Iron is mentioned last** — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads that placement as meaning iron may be used only as a last resort. A government may not exert its might to accomplish what is really the work of intellectual development; it may use force only when a party stands in the way of justice. "The main thing is to cultivate the minds of the people by educating them."

**"That Allah may know who helps Him and His messengers unseen."** Ibn Kathir: this means whose *intention* in carrying weapons is the defence of Allah's religion and His Messenger. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, following *Ruh ul-Maʿani*, explains that this is knowing "legally and outwardly": Allah knows everything pre-eternally, having pre-recorded it in the Book of Decrees; what the deed adds is that when a person performs it, the angels record it in his account, and so its legal manifestation becomes plainly apparent. Ibn Kathir closes on the point that keeps this from breeding self-importance: Allah gives victory to those who give victory and aid to Him — yet **Allah does not need mankind's help at all**. He ordered *jihad* to test people with each other.

## Ayah 26: the two fathers of prophecy

Ibn Kathir: since Allah sent Nuh (peace be upon him), **every prophet and messenger after him came from his offspring**; and every revealed Book and every messenger who received revelation after Ibrahim, the intimate friend of Allah (*Khalil*), came from Ibrahim's offspring. He cites the parallel wording of 29:27.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why these two names. **Nuh** stands first because he is a second Adam — all human beings after the Deluge were from his progeny. **Ibrahim** follows because he is the father of the prophets, recognised as an ideal by all the divine religions; out of the many branches of Nuh's progeny, his was the one singled out for prophethood.

Then the sentence turns: "**And among them there are some who are guided; but many of them are rebellious.**" Descent from prophets guarantees nothing. Ibn Kathir heads this whole section "Many of the Nations of the Prophets were Rebellious."

## Ayah 27: 'Isa, and the hearts of his followers

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the structure: after naming Nuh and Ibrahim, the whole chain of prophets is gathered up in "Then We made Our messengers follow them one after the other," and 'Isa is singled out at the end because he was the last among the Israelite prophets. Ibn Kathir adds that 'Isa prophesied the good news of the coming of Muhammad ﷺ — and the very next ayah, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, carries a pointed reference to the last of all prophets and his Shari'ah.

**"And We placed in the hearts of those who followed him compassion and mercy."** Ibn Kathir identifies these followers as the disciples, glossing *raʼfah* as compassion and tenderness, *rahmah* as mercy toward the creatures.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on the pair: generally treated as synonyms or near-synonyms, but here they stand side by side, so some lexicologists say *raʼfah* is stronger in degree. Others give a finer distinction: **raʼfah is to alleviate someone's calamity; rahmah is to give someone what he needs.** Since repelling harm normally comes before deriving benefit, *raʼfah* is named first. In the disciples this may mean tenderness among themselves, or kindness toward the entire creation of Allah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a comparison: in 48:29 the Companions are "compassionate among themselves" but are named first as "hard against the disbelievers" — the reason for the difference seeming to be that there were no laws of *jihad* in the Shari'ah of 'Isa, so no occasion arose for that severity. "Allah knows best."

## Monasticism: what it was, and what went wrong

**The word.** *Rahbaniyyah* is attributed to *ruhban*; *rahib* (singular) and *ruhban* (plural) mean **one who fears**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes what these fearful ones did: after 'Isa, transgression became common, and the kings and leaders publicly defied the laws of the Gospel; the scholars and righteous people who tried to stop them were put to death. Those who remained judged that they could neither stop the evil nor resist it, and that living in that society made it likely their own religion would be destroyed too. So they took upon themselves in earnest to give up all pleasures and comforts of this life, including the lawful ones: avoiding marriage, abandoning the effort to earn a livelihood and to build homes, taking to jungles, mountains and caves, or to a nomadic life, so as to protect their religion and practise it freely. They did all this out of fear of Allah, and so were called *ruhban*.

**The story behind the ayah.** Ibn Kathir records, from Ibn Jarir and Abu 'Abdur-Rahman An-Nasa'i — the wording being An-Nasa'i's — that Ibn 'Abbas said: kings after 'Isa changed the Tawrah and the Injil while there were still believers reciting the originals, reciting against them "And whosoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, such are the disbelievers" (5:44). A king summoned these reciters and threatened them with death unless they abandoned the original text for the corrupted version. They refused, and asked only to be let alone — one group requesting a narrow elevated tower they could ascend, another to go about in the land, a third homes in the deserts and secluded areas where they could dig wells and plant vegetables. Ibn 'Abbas said the ayah was revealed about this.

**A second narration.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a report of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, recorded by Ibn Kathir with reference to Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is reported to have said that the Children of Israel were split into seventy-two sects, of which only three were saved from punishment. The first faced the oppressors with whatever power they had, and were defeated and killed. A second, with even less fighting strength, conveyed the truth without caring for their lives and were killed — some ripped apart with saws, some burnt alive — bearing it for the sake of Allah's pleasure and attaining salvation. A third had no resources to fight the tyrants nor any way to keep their religion in that corrupt society, so they took to the jungles and mountains and became monks. **It is this third group the ayah speaks of.**

## What exactly is being criticised

Ibn Kathir states the criticism in two parts: **first**, they invented things in their religion that Allah did not legislate for them; **second**, they did not fulfil the requirements of what they themselves invented and claimed was a means of drawing near to Allah — "they did not abide by what they ordered themselves to do."

On "only to please Allah therewith," Ibn Kathir records **two opinions**: (1) they wanted to please Allah by inventing monasticism — the view of Sa'id bin Jubayr and Qatadah; (2) the sense is: We did not ordain that practice upon them; We ordained only that they seek what pleases Allah.

Because monasticism was introduced under forced circumstances, to protect their faith, **it was not reproachable in its origin**. But once a person imposes something on himself it becomes binding, and violating it is a sin — as with a vow: not obligatory before it is made, sinful to break after. Some monks began with the best of intentions; others could not endure the hardships and, once people believed in them and brought gifts and offerings, succumbed to the pursuit of material gain and physical pleasure — history, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says bluntly, bears ample testimony that monks who detested marriage fell into indecency.

**The word *ibtadaʿūhā*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds that *ibtidaʿ* here carries its **literal** sense of invention, not the technical or religious sense of *bid'ah* — a baseless belief or practice made part of the religion — which is denounced in the narration of the Prophet ﷺ, "Every religious innovation is deviation." (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites this narration without naming a collection.) Two arguments support the literal reading: first, context — monasticism is listed grammatically alongside *raʼfah* and *rahmah*, which are not evil qualities, and Allah would not have listed it beside them were it evil in itself. Second, Ibn Mas'ud's narration places the monks among the **saved**, which they could not be had they been guilty of religious innovation.

**Scholars differed here.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that those who held monasticism absolutely prohibited, such as **Qurtubi**, faced grammatical difficulties: they had to treat "and monasticism..." as a separate sentence with the verb understood as omitted, rather than part of the conjoined list. The reading Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adopts makes that construction unnecessary: the Qur'an rejects not their adoption of monasticism in principle, but their failure to keep it up and take care of its rights and obligations. (Mufti Muhammad Taqi Usmani notes that the ayah admits of two grammatical translations, and this discussion rests on the second.)

## Is monasticism forbidden outright?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distinguishes stages of "giving up some lawful things and pleasures":

1. **Treating a permissible thing as impermissible**, doctrinally or practically. This is distortion of religion and absolutely prohibited — the principle of 5:87, "do not prohibit the good things which Allah has made lawful to you."
2. **Giving something lawful up for a reason**, without turning it unlawful — avoiding a food because of illness, avoiding company lest one fall into lying and backbiting, dropping permissible things temporarily to suppress base desires. This is treatment of a spiritual disease, and when the treatment is over the restriction ends. Some spiritual guides ask a beginner to eat little, sleep little and mix little until balance (*i'tidal*) is attained and the *nafs* is under control, then have him give the exercise up. **This is not monasticism at all — it is taqwa**, required by the religion and practised by the Companions, their followers and the leaders in religion.
3. **Abstaining from something established by the Sunnah**, believing that giving it up carries more virtue and more reward. This is *ghuluww* — over-indulgence — which many Prophetic traditions prohibit.

The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said, "There is no monasticism in Islam," which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān applies to abandoning permissible things with the mistaken notion that it will bring reward. Judged by these categories: if the Children of Israel initiated monasticism to protect their religion, it falls under the second — righteousness. But the People of the Book were given to *ghuluww*; where they turned lawful into unlawful they fell under the first category and are guilty of the forbidden, and where they fall under the third, they are still guilty of something condemned. "Allah, the Pure and Exalted, knows best."

## The rahbaniyyah of this ummah

Ibn Kathir attaches here a hadith that reframes renunciation. **Imam Ahmad** recorded that Anas bin Malik said the Prophet ﷺ said: *Every Prophet has rahbaniyyah (monasticism); jihad in the cause of Allah, the Exalted and Most Honored, is the rahbaniyyah of this ummah.* **Al-Hafiz Abu Ya'la** collected the hadith with the wording *Every ummah has rahbaniyyah...* Our renunciation is not withdrawal into a cave but self-expenditure *within* the world in Allah's cause. Ibn Kathir also records, from **Imam Ahmad** alone, the advice Abu Sa'id Al-Khudri gave a man who sought it — advice he had himself sought from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: adhere to the *taqwa* of Allah, for it is the chief of all matters; fulfil the obligation of *jihad*, for it is the *rahbaniyyah* of Islam; and take care of remembering Allah and reciting the Qur'an, for it is your closeness in the heavens and your good fame on earth.

## Living it

**Justice is the point** — the declared purpose of every messenger, every Book, and the Balance itself. **Argument comes before force**: thirteen years of proof in Makkah before iron was drawn, and iron named last in the ayah. And **do not invent obligations for yourself, nor break the ones you take on** — the double criticism in ayah 27 cuts both ways. Running under it all is the refrain closing ayat 26 and 27: *many of them are rebellious.* Being born inside a guided lineage saves no one; answering the messenger does.

passages.title: Double mercy and a light to walk by
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat close Sūrat al-Ḥadīd with an invitation and a warning wrapped together: an open-armed call to those who already follow an earlier scripture to add faith in Muḥammad ﷺ to the faith they have, with a promise of a *doubled* portion of mercy, a light to walk by, and forgiveness (ayah 28) — and then, in ayah 29, the reason this promise is announced so publicly: so that the People of the Scriptures may know that they have no power whatsoever over the grace of Allah, that grace is in His Hand, to bestow on whomever He wills.

What holds the passage together is a single idea seen from two sides. Ayah 28 shows the grace being *given*. Ayah 29 shows that no one has any power over the giving of it.

## Who is being addressed

Ayah 28 opens with the Qur'an's most familiar address: **"O you who believe."** Normally that call summons the Muslims. Here something unusual is happening.

Ibn Kathīr recalls a hadith that **An-Nasā'ī collected from Ibn 'Abbās** that this ayah is about the People of the Scriptures who believe in Islam, and that they will earn double their reward if they do so. He notes that there is an ayah in **Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ** that supports this meaning, and adds that **Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, 'Utbah bin Abī Ḥakīm and others agreed with Ibn 'Abbās** in this, and that **Ibn Jarīr** preferred it.

Maʿārif ul Qur'ān draws out the grammar of that address. As a general rule, the Qur'an uses the vocative *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū* — "O those who believe" — for Muslims only, not for Jews or Christians; the expression used for them is *ahl al-kitāb*, People of the Book. Their believing in the Prophets Mūsā and 'Īsā (peace be upon them) is not tantamount to being "believers"; that requires believing in the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ. So why does the Qur'an here call them by the very title it usually withholds?

Maʿārif ul Qur'ān answers that the Qur'an deviates from its general rule here presumably because of what the concluding verse is doing: reminding the Christians that believing in the Prophet 'Īsā (peace be upon him) is not sufficient — that the *true meaning* of believing in him dictates that they should believe in the Last Prophet ﷺ. If they do, then they deserve to be called *alladhīna āmanū*, "those who believe." The address is, in effect, held out to them in advance: this is what you will be called, if you take the step.

That gives the two commands of ayah 28 their force. Ibn Kathīr's text renders them **"Have Taqwā of Allah, and believe in His Messenger"**; the passage translation renders the first as **"Fear Allah."** The one already called to stand in awe of Allah is being told what that now obliges: recognising the Messenger Allah has sent.

## "A double portion of His mercy"

The promise is *kiflayn min raḥmatih* — rendered by Ibn Kathīr's translator as "a double portion of His mercy," and by Maʿārif ul Qur'ān as "two shares of reward out of His mercy."

Maʿārif ul Qur'ān explains what the two shares are for. **The first** is on account of their having believed in the Prophet 'Īsā or Mūsā (peace be upon them) and followed their Sharī'ah. **The second** is for their believing in the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ and acting upon his Sharī'ah.

And it explains *why* this is such a striking gift. Jews and Christians were unbelievers until they believed in the Prophet ﷺ, and no worship of an unbeliever is acceptable. That would require that any action they had performed according to a previous Sharī'ah should go to waste. But this verse clarifies that when an unbeliever embraces Islam, all his good actions are restored — hence he is doubly rewarded. Nothing is written off.

**How large is a "portion"?** Ibn Kathīr preserves a small, vivid exchange. Sa'īd bin 'Abdul-'Azīz said that 'Umar bin al-Khaṭṭāb asked a Jewish rabbi: "What is the maximum a reward would be increased for you?" He replied: "A *Kifl* (portion) — which is about three hundred and fifty good merits." So 'Umar said: **"Praise be to Allah who gave us two Kifls."** Sa'īd then mentioned this very phrase of the ayah, *yu'tikum kiflayni min raḥmatih*, and said, "And the two Kifls on Friday are similar to that." **This was recorded by Ibn Jarīr.**

Notice what 'Umar's response is *not*. It is not a boast about Muslim merit. It is praise directed at the Giver. That is exactly the note ayah 29 will end on.

## Three who are paid twice

Ibn Kathīr cites a hadith from **Ash-Sha'bī, from Abū Burdah, from his father, from Abū Mūsā al-Ash'arī**, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Three will get their reward twice. A believer from the People of the Scriptures who has been a true believer in his Prophet and then believes in me, will get a double reward. A slave who fulfills Allah's rights and obligations as well as the duties of his master, will get a double reward. A person who has a slave-girl and he educates her properly and teaches her good manners properly (without violence) and then manumits and marries her, will get a double reward."

Ibn Kathīr states that this hadith **is recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs**.

What the three have in common, as the hadith describes them, is that each answers to two claims at once and answers both faithfully: two prophets, two sets of rights, or a position of authority over another turned into education, then freedom, then marriage. And in each case the reward is not merely counted once — it is doubled. The believer from the People of the Scriptures is the first named, which is precisely the reading of ayah 28 that Ibn 'Abbās gave.

## The parable of the labourers

To show that this doubling is *grace*, not arithmetic owed to anyone, Ibn Kathīr brings two versions of a parable.

The first, he says, is a hadith that **Imām Aḥmad recorded from 'Abdullāh bin 'Umar**, and he adds that **al-Bukhārī collected this hadith**. The Prophet ﷺ likened this community and the Jews and Christians to a person who employed some labourers and asked: who will work for me from the Dawn prayer until midday for one *Qīrāṭ* — a special weight of gold — each? So the Jews worked. Who will do the work from the Ẓuhr prayer to the time of the 'Aṣr prayer for one Qīrāṭ each? So the Christians worked. Then: who will do the work from the 'Aṣr prayer until sunset for *two* Qīrāṭ each? "You are those who did this work." The Jews and the Christians got angry and said, "We did more work, but got less wages." Allah said, "Have I been unjust to you with your reward?" They said, "No." So Allah said: **"Then it is My grace which I bestow on whomever I will."**

The second version **al-Bukhārī recorded from Abū Mūsā** — and Ibn Kathīr notes that **al-Bukhārī was alone in recording it**. Here a man employs labourers to work from morning until night for a known wage. They work until midday, then say, "We are not in need of the wages that you promised and our work was in vain." The man says, "Do not quit now, complete the rest of the work and yours will be the full wage I have fixed for it." They refuse and quit. He hires another batch on the wage he had promised the first, and they work until the time of the 'Aṣr prayer, then say, "Whatever we have done is in vain and we forfeit the wages you promised us." He says, "Complete your day's work, for only a small part of the day remains." They refuse too. He then employs another batch to work for the rest of the day, "and they worked until sunset and received the wages of the two former batches." The Prophet ﷺ concluded that this is an example of them — the Jews and Christians — and of those who accepted **this light**, which the text glosses as **Islam**.

Two things follow from these parables:

**First, the doubling is not a complaint against anyone's fairness.** In the parable itself the earlier workers are asked directly whether they were wronged in their reward, and they answer, "No." Their wage was exactly what was agreed. What upsets them is that someone else received more — which is a grievance against generosity, not against justice.

**Second, the day was offered whole to everyone.** In the second version the employer pleads with each group in turn to stay and finish and take the full wage; each time it is the workers who walk away. Only the last batch works to sunset — and they, the hadith says, "received the wages of the two former batches."

## "A light by which you shall walk"

The second gift in ayah 28 is *nūr* — "and He will give you a light by which you shall walk (straight)." The parable's closing words tell us what that light is: it ends by speaking of "those who accepted **this light**," glossed in Ibn Kathīr's text as **Islam**.

So the light is not decorative. It is *walking* light — the kind you need under your feet on a road, not the kind you admire. Taqwā and faith in the Messenger are asked for in the first half of the ayah; light on the path is what is handed back.

Ibn Kathīr sets alongside this another ayah:

> "O you who believe! If you have Taqwā of Allah, He will grant you a criterion, and will expiate for you your sins, and forgive you; and Allah is Owner of the great bounty." (8:29)

Line the two up and the same shape appears: taqwā → something to see by (there a criterion, here a light) → forgiveness → and the identical closing seal, **"Allah is the Owner of great bounty."**

And the third gift, which the ayah saves for last: **"And He will forgive you. And Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."** The promise does not end with reward and guidance; it ends with the past being covered over.

## Ayah 29: whose hand the bounty is in

"So that the People of the Scriptures may know that they have no power whatsoever over the grace of Allah, and that (His) grace is (entirely) in His Hand to bestow it on whomsoever He wills. And Allah is the Owner of great bounty."

**A grammatical note.** Maʿārif ul Qur'ān points out that the negative particle *lā* in this opening phrase is grammatically redundant — rhetorically it serves to emphasise the expression. Maʿārif ul Qur'ān accordingly renders the phrase simply: "so that the People of the Book may know." This is worth knowing if you are reading the Arabic and the words seem to fight the translation.

**What they are to know.** Ibn Kathīr glosses "they have no power whatsoever over the grace of Allah" as meaning: *so that they become sure that they cannot prevent what Allah gives, or give what Allah prevents.* Two directions, both closed. No one can veto a gift Allah has decided on, and no one can issue a gift Allah has withheld.

That is the answer to the objection voiced in the parable. If prophethood, scripture and favour ran on seniority, the earlier communities would have had a claim. But the ayah says the grace is in Allah's Hand — He bestows it on whomever He wills.

Maʿārif ul Qur'ān adds the practical conclusion for those addressed: the People of the Book need to know that faith in the Prophet 'Īsā (peace be upon him) is not necessarily faith in the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ, and in those circumstances they do not deserve any Divine grace unless they embrace faith in the Last Prophet ﷺ. Then it closes, as the classical scholars do: **"Allah, the Pure and Exalted, knows best!"**

## Living it

**Grace is never a possession to be defended.** The one deadly move in the parable is the workers' assumption that the yard belonged to them, so that another man's larger wage was a theft from their pocket. Ayah 29 is aimed at exactly this reflex — and it is a human reflex, not a Jewish or Christian one. A Muslim who resents that Allah has given someone else knowledge, wealth, ease of worship, or a beautiful turn to their life has drifted toward precisely the attitude this ayah corrects.

**Nothing sincere is wasted.** Maʿārif ul Qur'ān's point — that when a person embraces Islam all his good actions are restored to him — is a mercy worth holding on to. Someone entering Islam does not begin at zero with an erased life behind them.

**Notice the ones carrying two claims at once.** The hadith of the three doubly-rewarded names people whose obedience answers to more than one demand: the believer from the People of the Scriptures who believed in his Prophet and then in Muḥammad ﷺ, the slave who fulfils Allah's rights and his master's, the man who educated a slave-girl well, freed her and married her. In each case the hadith says the reward is doubled.

**And the response to being given much is 'Umar's response.** Told what the maximum increase in reward was in the rabbi's reckoning, he said, "Praise be to Allah who gave us two Kifls." Not *we earned it* — but *He gave it*. That is ayah 28 and ayah 29 held together in one sentence.

With these ayat the commentary on Sūrat al-Ḥadīd comes to an end. As Ibn Kathīr closes it: this is the end of the Tafsīr of Sūrat al-Ḥadīd — all praise is due to Allah, and all favours come from Him.
